topics.explain: Both can mean 'for', but they aren't interchangeable. Para points ahead to a goal: purpose (para aprender), recipient (es para ti), destination (salgo para Madrid), deadline (para el lunes). Por points to the cause or the route: reason (gracias por venir), through/along (por la calle), exchange (por diez euros), parts of the day (por la mañana). Watch out: 'thanks for' is always gracias por.
examples: Estudio español para hablar con mi familia.
I study Spanish (in order) to talk to my family.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Estudio español ___ hablar con mi familia de México.
questions.why: Purpose ('in order to') is para + infinitive. Por + infinitive would give a reason ('because of'), not a goal.
Thanking someone for something always uses por: gracias por el regalo. Para marks a goal or recipient, not the reason for thanks.

topics.explain: Gustar, encantar (to love), interesar and doler (to hurt) work 'backwards': the thing is the subject and the person is an indirect pronoun (me, te, le, nos, les). Use a singular verb for one thing or an infinitive (me gusta bailar), a plural verb for plural things (me duelen los pies). Add a + person for clarity: a Ana le encanta. Watch out: 'I like' is me gusta, never 'yo gusto'.
examples: A mis padres les gustan las montañas.
I have a headache. (lit. My head hurts me.)

questions.q: Fill in the blank: A nosotros ___ encantan los faroles.
questions.why: The indirect pronoun matches the person: a nosotros > nos. The verb (encantan) agrees with los faroles.
With doler the body part is the subject, so the verb agrees with it: los pies (plural) > duelen. Spanish uses the article (los pies), not 'mis'.

topics.topic: Irregular preterite stems: tuve, estuve, pude, vine
topics.explain: Many everyday verbs have an irregular preterite stem and special endings with no accent: -e, -iste, -o, -imos, -ieron. Tener > tuv-, estar > estuv-, poder > pud-, poner > pus-, querer > quis-, venir > vin-, hacer > hic- (hizo). After j, -ieron becomes -eron: dijeron, trajeron. Watch out: 'tuvó' and 'pudó' are wrong; these forms never take a written accent.
examples: We were in Valencia for two days.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: El sábado mis primos ___ a la boda.
questions.why: Venir has the irregular stem vin- and takes -ieron for 'they': vinieron.
Irregular preterites with special stems never take a written accent: tuvo, not 'tuvó'.

topics.topic: Obligation: tener que, hay que, deber
topics.explain: Tener que + infinitive = to have to (a personal obligation): tengo que trabajar. Hay que + infinitive = one has to / it's necessary (general, no subject): hay que reservar. Deber + infinitive = should / must (advice or duty): debes descansar. Watch out: don't drop the que after tener ('tengo trabajar' is wrong), and hay que never changes for the person.
examples: I have to buy a light bulb.
Si hay niebla, hay que caminar despacio.
If there's fog, you have to walk slowly.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Mañana yo ___ levantarme a las seis.
questions.why: A personal obligation is tener que + infinitive. Tengo without que is wrong, hay que has no personal subject (so not with levantarme), and deber takes no que.

questions.q: What does 'Hay que llegar a las ocho' mean?
options: One has to (you have to) arrive at eight.
There is someone who arrives at eight.
questions.why: Hay que + infinitive expresses a general obligation without naming who: 'you have to / it's necessary to'.

topics.topic: Negative words: no ... nada, nadie, nunca
topics.explain: Spanish uses double negatives. If nada, nadie or nunca comes after the verb, put no before the verb: no veo a nadie (I don't see anyone), no dice nada (it doesn't say anything). If the negative word comes first, drop the no: nadie respondió, nunca llego tarde. Watch out: 'I don't see anything' is no veo nada, not 'no veo algo'.
examples: Tu cuaderno no dice nada más.
Your notebook doesn't say anything else.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: En la calle no había ___.
questions.why: After no + verb, Spanish uses the negative word: no había nadie (there wasn't anyone). Alguien is for positive sentences.

questions.q: Which sentence correctly says 'I never arrive late'?
questions.why: When nunca comes before the verb, there is no 'no'. (No llego nunca tarde is also correct, with no before the verb and nunca after it.)

topics.explain: Hace + time with the preterite means 'ago': llegué hace dos años = I arrived two years ago. For something that started in the past and is still true, Spanish normally uses the present with desde hace or hace ... que: vivo aquí desde hace dos años = I've lived here for two years. Watch out: English uses 'have lived'; Spanish prefers the present here, and 'ago' is never 'antes'.
examples: Mi hermana cambió de número hace dos días.
My sister changed her number two days ago.
Vivo en Santiago desde hace un año.
I've lived in Santiago for a year.
Hace diez minutos que te espero.
I've been waiting for you for ten minutes.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Llegué a Madrid ___ tres semanas.
questions.why: Hace + time after a preterite means 'ago': llegué hace tres semanas. Desde means 'since', and 'antes tres semanas' is not Spanish ('three weeks earlier' would be tres semanas antes).

questions.q: What does 'Estudio español desde hace un año' mean?
options: I studied Spanish a year ago.
I will study Spanish for a year.
I studied Spanish for a year, but I stopped.
I have been studying Spanish for a year.
questions.why: Present tense + desde hace = an action that started in the past and continues now: 'I have been studying ... for a year'.
